The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements and applications of creating two-dimensional measurement maps using
Laser Doppler Vibrometry in a remote setting. A comparative analysis has been
conducted on different methods for analyzing the frequency and phase response of
samples, which were tested by exciting them with either one or multiple beams of
light while subjecting them to either a single or multiple-point excitation.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of $\Phi'$ are all bipartite.  Additionally, we develop a version of the Trefoil theorem applicable to first-order sentences with multiple variables over relations that are binary and symmetric in nature.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is examined in the context of electron transmission microscopy. A programmable electrostatic phase plate is capable of modifying a transmission electron microscope's (TEM) phase contrast and spherical aberration correction capabilities by compensating for the C_s value of a celem. A celem, an electrostatic phase plate designed to compensate for C_s, enables high-resolution imaging of a variety of sample types without the need for phase-contrast defocus. It is estimated that a programmable electrostatic phase plate can accurately compensate for C_s within a spatial frequency range of approximately 0.08 to 0.13 Å$^{-1}, which corresponds to a potential resolution of 7.7 to 12.5 Å. To validate these findings, the simulations were validated using atomic positions from a well-studied structure, beta-barrel bacteriorhodopsin whose high-resolution crystal structure is well-documented.

Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper.

This study focuses on determining the general equation for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size, denoted as $|P_n^{d}|$. The aim is to establish a recursive relationship for the combination of binomial coefficients $\binom{n}{d}$. Various special case formulas have also been explored and are presented, including the computation of $|P_n^{d}|$ when $d$ equals $2$, $3$, and a multiple of $n$.

This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin in 2010, as an attempt to resolve the singularity present in the classical Schwarzschild black hole through quantum gravity principles. We begin with the classical perturbation equation for the black hole and then derive the corresponding equation of motion for the perturbed field in the context of the polymer model. Upon solving the equation, we obtain the characteristic frequencies of the perturbation, which exhibit nontrivial dependence on the parameter $\lambda_{C}$. Our findings demonstrate that the perturbed fields in these polymer black holes experience quantum influences and behave differently from their classical counterparts.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed expression. Additionally, cross-sentence prosodic cues are incorporated into each sentence through a novel low-level linker and a harmonic harmonic coding module. Through extensive datasets including CleanSpeech and VCTK, as well as a real-world recording at a tech event, experimental results demonstrate the superiority of MaskedSpeech in terms of naturalness and semantic divergence, surpassing non-contextual synthesis systems such as FastSpeech 2.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a framework that maintains the full model's predictive accuracy while significantly reducing computational complexity. This approach is supported by theoretical validation showing that our selection method identifies relevant variables and structures with high probability. We've developed multiple selection strategies and evaluated their effectiveness through simulations and real-world applications, demonstrating the benefits of our method in variable selection and structure selection models.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of various defensive techniques. Although these inputs primarily exhibit a specific form of malicious behavior - responding to specific attacks in the same manner without triggering others - previous studies have investigated their underlying causes and potential ramifications. This work aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the potential consequences that arise from the unique vulnerability displayed by DNNs when encountering benign inputs. The results indicate that this vulnerability has significant implications for the safety of public and private data. Due to the complexities associated with assessing the potential danger it poses when multiple adversaries are involved, we have formulated a hypothetical scenario in which multiple hackers collaborate. Under these conditions, the level of cooperation between adversaries has a profound effect on the vulnerability it poses. Overall, our research has shed light on an underappreciated aspect of the danger presented by the unique vulnerability displayed by DNNs.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly on social media where individuals with personality traits like high neuroticism are more inclined to engage with conspiracy content. Levels of conspiracy engagement and sharing on Twitter are particularly influenced by the recipient's belief in climate change. This project uses Natural Language Processing to analyze over 10 million climate change related tweets from 2017 to 2021, discovering a correlation between high climate change belief and the popularity of conspiracy theories, along a decline in proposed science-based facts, especially from the most effective climate change activists, contrary to expected trends.

A study focusing on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions that featured a final state with large missing transverse momentum and either two jets or lepton pairs, each with a mass range of 2-12 GeV, 20-100 GeV, or 100-120 GeV. comparisons between measured outcomes and predictions based on dark matter models, along with predictions based on standard models, were made in this study. Based on comparisons with expected outcomes, lower limits on the mass of scalar and pseudoscalar mediators were determined to be 140 GeV, while for vector mediators, the mass limit depends on the coupling of the mediator to dark matter, ranging from 100 GeV for a coupling of 0.15 to 140 GeV for a coupling of 0.15. Additionally, this study reported exclusion limits for various leptoquark and R-particle models, while the model-dependent exclusion limits for pseudoscalar and vector mediators were also established.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon previous work for single treatment scenarios, we expand the unit treatment framework to accommodate multiple unordered treatments without relying on continuous instruments. For both observed and unobserved treatment effect models, we develop identification and partial identification results. We also propose new estimators for observed treatment effects and their performance appears superior than the traditional estimator proposed by Heckman and Waidyaratne (2019). Simulation studies demonstrate that our estimator's performance appears better than the traditional one proposed by Heckman and Waidaratne when handling multiple unordered treatments.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of particles like electrons, protons, and even exotic particles such as hyperons and positrons, creating difficult-to-stable particles in large numbers has always been a major challenge in particle physics research.
However, a recent breakthrough involving the use of laser light to accelerate particles offers a new, exciting opportunity to study rare particles like antimatter and position states of deuterons as beam particles.
In our study, we investigate the feasibility of utilizing these rare particles in high-energy physics research by conducting simulations with the Deeper Inelastic Scattering Experiment, or DESE, in a virtual experiment environment.
Our DESE setup involves collisions between projectiles and a deuterium target, which allows us to compute scattering cross-sections using the Monte Carlo program, MC ENEPY.
In order to assess the potential data collection rates, we calculated scattering cross-sections and estimated achievable data collection rates, which indicate that collecting sufficient statistics for further analysis is achievable with current experimental facilities.
Overall, our findings demonstrate that obtaining data rates required for in-depth analysis of particle collisions involving rare particle beams and deuterium targets is feasible with existing experimental facilities.

Most of a young star cluster's stars reside in close, weakly interacting three-body systems, which may lead to the formation of an accretion disk. This work focuses on the behavior of these disks and how they affect how these systems gain mass. Using 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations, this study investigates how mass is accreted by these systems and how mass ratio variations impact mass accumulation. Results show that differential mass accumulation is common in these disks, but it is not solely dependent on how the system varies over time. Rather, it is also heavily influenced by the mass ratio between the system's outer components, which in turn affects the disk's structure and stability. This suggests that variable three-body systems can lead to mass accumulation patterns that are similar to those seen in systems with stable, equal-mass configurations. On the other hand, systems with significantly unequal mass between their outer components may lead to uniform mass accumulation, but only if they are surrounded by an accretion disk with a specific structure and orientation. This suggests that systems without accretion disks or with unusually shaped disks may also exhibit uniform mass accumulation, regardless of their time variability. This research highlights the intricate relationship between young star clusters and how they gain mass through various factors that are influenced by both time variability and mass ratios.

This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial configurations. Notably, our research uncovers an unexpected form of isotropic expansion for the universe, even in the absence of spherical symmetry. We ultimately present precise solutions to the Einstein's equations, along with examples of both vacuum and matter-filled spacetimes, including those with spatially periodic gravitational fields.

This paper introduces a novel image segmentation approach, combining image restoration and decomposing segmentation tasks. We acknowledge the limitations of current models in handling real-world images with various distortions. To address this, our model integrates a multi-task learning framework, optimizing both restoration and segmentation. This approach leads to the development of an end-to-end framework, resulting in the TIAS method. TIAS employs a specialized head to decompose the input image into relevant components, each restored separately by our proposed multi-fidelity image prior restoration network. Introducing fidelity as a new task, our method enables the model to focus on its primary objectives while achieving state-of-the-art results. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding significant improvements in both segmentation and distortion removal.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are highly luminous at X-ray and gamma-ray wavelengths, and by analyzing their electromagnetic spectrum, we can determine the properties of their central black holes, including mass and spin. A research method involves using the General Relativity Semianalytical code to model the black hole's spin and accretion disk, and fit this to observed AGN spectra. This technique allows for efficient estimation of angular momentum, as well as a thorough understanding of the influence of black hole parameters on spectrum features. It also provides a way to assess the reliability of inferred parameters, and offers a potential approach to AGN classification, such as identifying high black hole spin values, which may correspond to type I AGN.

Creating intelligent systems inspired by the human brain, known as neuromorphic systems, is gaining significant attention in the research community. The complexity of brain-like systems demands high-performance computing power, making them unique among other domain-specific systems. The absence of a high-performance open-source Python emulator hinders the development of brain-inspired models in Python, a widely popular language. To address this challenge, actionable Neuron was developed, a scalable and efficient Python emulator capable of handling large-scale brain-inspired systems. This study presents a performance evaluation of actionable Neuron and compares it with other state-of-the-art neural network emulators. The results indicate that actionable Neuron can handle large brain-inspired systems efficiently, boasting a large memory capacity and fast execution speed, while also offering scalable performance through partitioning and distribution across multiple CPUs.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by the massive ejection of plasma from a star due to small-scale strong radio bursts. The evolution of this phenomenon can be divided into distinct phases, each exhibiting specific patterns. We have obtained high-sensitivity observations of the solar type-I noise storm associated with a star flare on July 29, 2012, using the Nancay 260-ft radio telescope. These observations were analyzed across 12 frequency channels of 1.55-MHz bandwidth, spanning 22.5 to 30.0 GHz in a 400-MHz range. The data were analyzed every 16 seconds and processed every 10 seconds for a 3.2-hour duration preceding the solar flare and up to 2.3 hours after it. The data revealed a distinct source in a 1000-km square area, associated with a microflare, exhibiting two modes of evolution. The first mode involved horizontal source expansion and vertical movement towards the star's surface. The second mode involved rotation of the type-I noise beam. Additionally, the data supported hypotheses on plasma density distributions in the star's 100-R radius area and beam width as functions of density.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic energy carrying cloud with a Schwarzschild black hole and its surrounding Bondi sphere of influence is investigated. By employing a combination of symmetries and the perturbation method, we focus on understanding how angular momentum and entropy in the cloud affect mass accretion onto the black hole. Our results show that the merging of a purely kinetic and entropy-free cloud with a black hole results in a reduced mass accretion due to the formation of an angular barrier preventing radial mass flow. Conversely, we find that the inclusion of entropy in merging clouds can significantly increase mass accretion by a factor of around 1.5, likely due to entropic effects on pressure. However, the overall mass accretion rate in these cloud mergers remains well below that in the general relativity based models.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A long-term survey of Orion's massive star population has been established with the primary goal of monitoring their variability and identifying the impact of the Orion expanding wave on their development. A comprehensive analysis of years of photometric data for 31 sources, identified in the Orion cluster with the most similar characteristics, has been presented. The results show that out of observed variations in magnitude, only a small portion can be attributed to the Orion expanding wave. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of spectral requirements for seven specific sources shewed that most variances in source properties can be explained by their discovery in different years. What's more, a significant discovery was made that stars as massive as those found in the Orion cluster can be discovered outside of similar environments in other regions, indicating complex inter-system relationships.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper aging and environmental factors, often exhibit discoloration, stains, tears, and pixelation that severely impair readability. This study proposes a novel, end-to-end approach for restoring this information using a multi-scale autoencoder. By incorporating image enhancement and reconstruction modules, the framework effectively utilizes spatial size mappings to mitigate distortion. We evaluated the algorithm on a diverse collection of pages featuring old documents, calligraphic scripts, and historical papers, and the results showed significant improvements in image quality, which in turn slightly enhanced the readability of the handwritten content.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered the way information is shared and accessed. As a result, accessing data has become more convenient. This study introduces a method to easily convert ID card information into a computer-understandable format. It combines a cutting-edge image conversion technique with a advanced recognition system to process ID card images. This system uses Python to recognize Chinese ID cards based on the TML method, which allows it to extract relevant information from ID card images. We have also developed a way to verify the accuracy of the extracted data. A comparative analysis was performed with other popular ID card recognition techniques, and the results show that our proposed system outperforms them in terms of speed and reliability.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable data transmission a significant challenge. The effectiveness of OFDM as a suitable transmission technique is contingent on accurate channel estimation. Due to resource and complexity limitations, utilizing a single-carrier approach instead of MRC for combining diversity in ODSU protocols is a more feasible option. However, this necessitates reduced parallelism, thereby necessitating an increased number of pilots for precise channel tracking. The current method of uniform pilot placement proves to be inefficient, prompting an investigation into its alternatives. The type of channel and system parameters significantly influence the need for pilots, thereby potentially allowing for their strategic allocation. This protocol aims to identify optimal pilot positions by addressing two key considerations: equal error probabilities and a unified bit error rate. The research identifies conditions under which non-uniform pilot allocation yields beneficial outcomes, providing valuable insights for future vehicle-to-vehicle communication systems, particularly in scenarios involving wideband ODSU channels.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is a highly complex task, as the system struggles to interpret ambiguous images with ambiguous color, and this challenge is further compounded by dataset biases. The current state-of-the-art models rely on multi-step processes that are expensive to run and have difficulty generalizing to unfamiliar images. The model described in this paper addresses these limitations with efficient, accurate, and robust performance in colorization. The model utilizes the DINO self-supervised vision transformer pre-trained on the COCOCap captioning dataset. The code for this model is available on GitHub.

We've developed a numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without backpropagation, an approach rooted in Tannery's theorem. This method enables the precise determination of weights at each layer of a neural network. By exploiting the properties of the Heaviside function and applying a tailored quadrature rule, we can efficiently compute neural weights. The proposed method is particularly suited to certain types of boundary value problems, achieving a convergence rate of O(1/n^(1.5)) with proposed optimizations. The versatility of this approach allows it to handle problems involving smooth and discontinuous solutions, even under noisy conditions. The method's performance is illustrated through various numerical experiments, demonstrating its efficiency and adaptability.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in its first year of operation. This document outlines the panel's organizational structure, recent activities, and plans for the near future.

Confining modes at a boundary between two plates has been achievable through plasmonics, 
which leads to strong light confinement under certain conditions. 
In electromagnetism, this is not fully attainable due to a long-standing puzzle, 
despite being possible in other areas. 
We have discovered that at the boundary of two specially designed electromagnetic structures, 
strong wave phenomena occur that result in extremely high mode confinement. 
These wave phenomena have not been previously observed in electromagnetism and are known 
as line waves. 
These line modes have lower long-standing criteria for existence and can occur by combining 
two passive structures, which is a distinct feature. 
We have found that these line modes can lead to very high light confinement and have 
demonstrated this by creating a device that can convert these line modes into visible light. 
These line modes also have additional characteristics, 
including the ability to propagate horizontally and change direction based on their geometry, 
which are useful for developing new types of light-converting devices.

One of the most effective approaches for building intelligent robotic systems is learning across multiple autonomous agents. This method excels at resolving complex problems such as perception, cognition, and action across multiple levels of autonomy. However, traditional multi-agent learning techniques often struggle with critical issues when applied to robotic systems. These challenges include handling high-dimensional sensory and motor data, dealing with delayed and noisy feedback, and integrating learning with real-time control. This course aims to introduce students to multi-agent learning in real-time across diverse robotic platforms. It emphasizes the design and development of such systems using state-of-the-art machine learning algorithms and covers multi-perception, multi-object recognition, collaborative navigation, and shared social skills. By leveraging these techniques, students can create advanced robotic robotic systems that respond to human gestures and voice, and perform advanced tasks within their environments.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction and results in extremely large estimation variances. To overcome these limitations, a specific alternative strategy for bias reduction was implemented.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph construction are crucial areas within the realm of semantic understanding, yet existing methods often fall short due to their inability to effectively capture long-range dependencies and transfer learning across diverse domains, resulting in suboptimal performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that integrates a self-attention mechanism for relation modeling, employs a multi-task learning approach with shared encoder and domain-adaptive graph convolutional networks to capture long-range dependencies, and incorporates a data augmentation strategy by constructing a knowledge graph for enhanced representation learning. Experimental evaluations in the 2021 Chinese Area of NLP Evaluation show that our method achieved a 57.74% F1-score in the 2021 CNER task and 44.01% F1-score in the remote dependency parsing task, with a corresponding 4.10% and 1.44% improvement, respectively, compared to the baseline models. Additionally, we report 4.10% and 1.44% improvements over the best existing methods in the 2020 CNER and remote dependency parsing evaluations. The open-source implementation of our framework is available at the provided GitHub link.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been used to solve the N-dimensional Radial Dirac equation for the N-dimensional anisotropic harmonic oscillator model, which models the quark gluon plasma during plasma cooling. This method yielded closed-form solutions for the energy levels and wave functions, which were then used to investigate the impact of anisotropy on spin-splitting in N-dimensional space. It was discovered that anisotropy causes significant spin-splitting in N-dimensional space, which was used to study the properties of N-dimensional quarkonium in N-dimensional quark gluon plasma. Furthermore, this study investigated the effects of anisotropy and spatial dimension on the dissociation temperature of quarkonia such as $J/\Psi$, $\Upsilon$, $B_c$, and $W'$ in N-dimensional space. It was found that anisotropy leads to earlier quarkonium dissociation and that this effect is more pronounced in lower N dimensions. Notably, our model has the capability to study the dissociation of quarkonia in N-dimensional space, which has not been explored in previous research.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the gamma-terbium ruthenite, Tb3RuO7, based on neutron powder diffraction, single-crystal magnetization, and powder susceptibility measurements, which revealed a complex mixture of magnetic configurations. In the sample, Ru1 and Ru2 moments were found to adopt different order patterns, termed A and B, respectively, at temperatures below 15 K. These configurations, however, cannot be fully accounted for by a simple representation, but it was observed that they could arise from an arrangement of additional C-type ordered moments within three distinct triangular planes. Furthermore, this study also investigated the magnetic transitions within Tb3RuO7 and found that, in addition to two well-known magnetic fields required to induce transitions between Ta, AC, and AF states, an intermediate state involving an AC state was identified, labeled AC/AF.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have primarily been tailored to handle a single signal
or incorporate external information, limiting their general application. We
introduce a novel periodic MLp layer and a dual-MLP framework, which is
suited for processing consecutive data sequences like videos or audio. We
investigate the performance of this layer and explore strategies to
train both components simultaneously, minimizing memory usage. Experiments
show that our system outperforms recently developed models in compression
tasks on videos and sequences of images, while also demonstrating efficacy
with moving objects in a sequence.

We introduce a novel, general approach that integrates adaptation and semi-supervised learning to tackle the problem of covariate shift. The method relies on semi-supervised information from a subset of labeled data, as well as a broader set of unlabeled data points. A key aspect of our approach is the development of a novel regularization technique that utilizes low-rank matrices and the exponential of entropy. The experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art covariate shift adaptation methods that employ only unlabeled data and are comparable to methods that utilize full labeled data.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in this number field as $d$ changes. The research focuses on the identification of generators for $\mathcal{P}$-principal ideals that arise from the resolution of equations of the form $x^3 - dx = y^2$ within an elliptic curve. The investigation also involves examining the height of these generators, denoted by $h(\alpha)$ where $\alpha = \frac{B + E\sqrt[3]{d}}{(2F + G\sqrt[3]{d})\zeta_3^s}$, in relation to the genus field of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$. As $d$ grows, the dominant terms of the lattice minima $A$, $B$, $B^\sigma$ and $B^{\sigma^2}$ are analyzed and expressed as Laurent polynomials in terms of the genus invariants $c$, $e$, $e^\sigma$ and $e^{\sigma^2}$. A groundbreaking technique in particle physics, known as the top tagger, relies heavily on a specific type of deep neural network. However, this method is limited by its inability to utilize significant information about how jets behave on a local scale. In an effort to overcome this limitation, researchers have developed an enhanced method of connecting layers within the network, incorporating advanced analytical variables. This method shows remarkable results in increasing the accuracy of detecting complex structures within jets, reaching a significant performance milestone of $70\%$ accuracy with minimal false positives.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, specifically those adapted for r, which reflects the difference between dividing each set into exactly q subsets and ensuring each subset has at least r elements, and basic dividing where some subsets can be empty. This updated version of Stirling numbers obeys a specific recurrence relation that involves combinations of r, and we derive a corresponding identity that involves these numbers with varying subset counts. Additionally, this special case of dividing into subsets without overlap is shown to be consistent with existing theories when r equals one.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties were computed symbolically and efficiently, thanks to reduced space group symmetry and an adjusted coordinate system for maximizing computation speed. When possible, pre-calcured matrices and character tables, specific to layer symmetries, were used. These properties include layer space vector transformations, tensor irreducible representations, and invariants. Precomputed data, character tables, and other relevant information are hosted on the International Centre for Diffraction Research website for public access.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It is established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories. Specifically, when the manifold is of compact type, it must be an algebraic torus over a flat, simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold. Furthermore, Laplace's equation for the momentum operator implies that the manifold, in compact types, is composed of multiple flat components.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is the proposed compound symmetry, the momentum of the complex scalar field, $\sigma$, acts as a Nambu-Goldstone boson from a complex adjoint of the $Sp(6)$ group. The target manifold's coordinates are composed of these fields, and they are subject to a constraint that is a generalization of the basic constraint. The components of $\sigma$ at the Standard Model level include a complex $t$-beta and a real $t$-scalar, and a potential that is invariant under $U(1)_Y \times SU(2)_L$ and includes terms that are 4-Dim, 5-Dim, and 6-Dim in terms of these fields is calculated using an effective Lagrangian. This is done without a $t$-scalar vacuum expectation value, and a $U(1)_P$ pseudo symmetry is found to protect the $t$-scalar and give it a small mass as a result. The model has a predicted natural upper limit for the $t$-scalar mass of approximately 1250 GeV.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through the use of VPPMs, speculative design highlights hidden concepts and emerging trends within VR interaction, which can be applied to VPPMs to identify potential risks. This approach aids in the development of a comprehensive vulnerability framework, which serves as a guide for VR interaction design, collaboration between VR designers and physical designers, and future research into VPPM-based interactions.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have revealed the existence of massive core fragments, puzzling given the smaller masses of typical core masses. We've developed a one-dimensional code to study the mass distribution of these core fragments during binary star formation. Our calculations show that the total mass of a parent core has a significant impact on the mass and number of formed fragments, with more massive cores producing heavier and numerous fragments, whereas less massive cores tend to produce fewer and lighter fragments. Consequently, the total mass of the core can influence the mass distribution of the formed fragments, explaining the observed overabundance of massive binary fragments. We've found that short-range gravitational interactions can synchronize the periodic mass ejection from protostars, leading to a small mass excess in one of the fragments. We've also discovered that core fragmentation can result in mass ratios as small as 0.1, but that variable mass ejections can enhance the mass ratio to as high as 0.9 under certain conditions. This finding supports the hypothesis that the observed distribution of binary fragments with a wide range of mass ratios can be explained by the total mass of the parent core.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') as a method for extracting features from datasets. It either surpasses or stabilizes the performance of several existing ICA methods in a range of scenarios. The proposed framework integrates the benefits of three established techniques: the m-arcsinh transformation method, the kernel-based approach, and the FastICA algorithm. By combining these components, it addresses the limitations of these methods and enhances their ability to handle data non-linearity. While the transformation method and the kernel method are effective in some cases, they are sensitive to the severity of non-linearity. The proposed framework offers more consistent outcomes, especially when analyzing the non-linearity of simulated data. Furthermore, the inclusion of FastICA as a refinement step improves the quality of extracted features. The proposed framework also exhibits superior clustering accuracy compared to several existing methods, as confirmed by a comparison with standard approaches. Additionally, an explanation of how to implement the proposed framework within the Python environment is provided, including the creation of a library with corresponding functions and tests.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide insight into the relational versus circuit proof systems' relationship as explored in prior research.

A subring collection in a ring is an extensive set that can reduce the ring's size using its own elements. The minimum number of subrings needed to reduce a ring is known as its covering number. In this research, the author determines the covering numbers for full linear groups of sizes $p^n$ and $p^n + 1$, where $p$ is a prime and $n$ is a natural number, in the linear ring of integers modulo $2^{n+1}$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on current events and topics. Despite the benefits of connecting with social media, verifying the accuracy of information proves challenging due to multiple contributing factors. To address this issue, we propose a systematic approach for automated fact-checking, incorporating a knowledge graph-based model to verify claims by analyzing associated entities and evaluating their veracity. This proposed knowledge graph fact_checker leverages entity type, textual content, entity relations, entity values, entity values' categories, and employs Knowledge Graph Embeddings to fact-check assertions. This model capitalizes on existing knowledge graphs to link real-world entities to claims, enabling accurate verification even when information is ambiguous or involves new entities not present in knowledge graphs. In experiments using the Strategy Tactics International Fact-Checking Partnership dataset, we obtained an F1 score of 0.73, outperforming current baseline models.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The existing approaches social media analysis focuses on particular events or aspects, which restricts their general applicability. To this end, we introduce a new system, ProtoEvent, that automatically generates event representations from social media data streams and pinpoints the current relevance of those events. By leveraging the power of social graphs, our system relies solely on unlabelled social media data to learn event representations in a self-supervised manner, thus avoiding the need for manual labelling. Empirical results demonstrate that ProtoEvent generalizes well to various events and accurately predicts trending events over time and space.

We've introduced a new multi-dimensional tool, the weighted skew-spectrum, which offers richer information about the cosmos and more precise parameter estimates when compared to one-dimensional data. This skew-spectrum can be seen as an extension of the power spectrum concept, capturing both real-space and redshift-space data in higher dimensions. By using numerical simulations from the Illustris-TNG series, which model a realistic 321 Megaparsec region of the cosmos, we have found that the two-dimensional skew-spectrum can be accurately measured from an optical dataset like the Viper B-band, down to the $3\times10^{-3}$ level at the largest scales and $10^{-4}$ at smaller ones. Furthermore, we have found that estimating fundamental cosmological parameters like the density of matter, the nature of dark energy, and the fluctuation amplitude in a specific dataset like Viper would be more precise with the help of two-dimensional skew-spectra, compared to relying solely on one-dimensional redshift-space power spectra, especially for specific parameters like the fluctuation amplitude of a specific dataset like Viper which would be estimated to a 1-3% accuracy level.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to train a Bayesian neural network to resist attacks. Evaluation on standard datasets demonstrated that our method surpasses traditional P-DNN and standard BNN in providing certifiable guarantees, and comparable to P-DNN in adversarial performance. Furthermore, we introduced a record on the strongest certifiable BNN.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the temporal and spatial diffusion of a prominent rumor, analyzing the underlying drivers. As the study's foundation, we constructed a hybrid model, blending a spatial agent-based model with characteristics of small-world networks, and an temporal Susceptible- susceptible to denial, finally susceptible, susceptible to denial, and susceptible model, designed for complex network environments. Our results in synthetic networks highlighted the impact of parameter and network structure on disease spread, also indicating complete disease eradication under specific thresholds. Additionally, our analysis in a real internet data environment identified key characteristics of a prominent rumor, uncovering its rapid propagation within a short time frame and among a large population. According to content and structure analysis, we concluded that the rapid spread of the rumor can be attributed to its highly confusing and emotionally manipulative content, along with emotional network structure. Furthermore, simulation experiments demonstrated that limiting the directness of information dissemination significantly reduces the full coverage of the manipulated population.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification accuracy, focusing on various reduction methods such as manifold learning, linear projection, and nonlinear projection. Using 15 different datasets, we examined the performance of reduction methods in conjunction with a classification algorithm. Our analysis revealed that for both continuous and discrete compression rates, increasing the number of transformed pixel features significantly impacts classification performance, with more quantitative information generally leading to better accuracy up to a certain threshold. Furthermore, we found that nonlinear projection methods often yield the highest classification performance, followed by manifold learning and linear projection techniques.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors, but they are also criticized for their excessive size. The second most effective model reduction method after pruning is finding distinctive "neural network tickets." We have used a genetic algorithm to search for these "network tickets" by evolving sub-networks. Our experiments were conducted on several problems including image classification with VGG16, ResNet-50, and Bert-Large models on the ImageNet dataset, as well as semantic segmentation with VGG16, VGG16-SE, VGG16-BN, VGG16-SB, VGG16-SB SE, VGG16-SB SE BN models, and the VOC2012 dataset. We also attempted to isolate a single neural network ticket for the image classification utilizing ResNet50 on the ImageNet dataset, as well as separating a network ticket for the semantic segmentation utilizing VGG16 on the VOC2012 dataset that was devoid of data augmentations. Our results indicate that it is feasible to isolate a sub-network with top-performing weights by applying genetic algorithm searches on different problems including classification, the use of data augmentations, and semantic segmentation.

A novel prediction method, PCS-Pro, has been developed to calculate amide proton chemical shift deviations for proteins within an insoluble environment. This has been accomplished by creating two sub-models, one to determine the deviation of isotropic chemical shifts and another for axial chemical shift deviation. Subsequently, these models were used to generate predicted amide proton chemical shift deviations. Furthermore, PCS-Pro was integrated into BAXS to reconstruct protein x-ray structure. This approach was applied to predict the chemical shift deviations and three-dimensional structures of TFIID and SH3BPR PDB4OXK. Evaluation of the PCS-Pro model using cross-validation and comparison with the Axon PCS data confirmed its reliability. Notably, the structure generated by combining PCS-Pro and BAXS provided a more accurate representation compared to existing methods, as demonstrated by lower RMSA values. Examination of the integration interface revealed key interactions between SH3BPR residues and the X-ray crystal, enabling three-dimensional structure reconstruction. This method holds promise for uncovering the fundamental mechanisms behind protein folding in response to x-ray beams.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is a crucial decision when designing a learning algorithm for a specific task. In this research, we will discuss our approach to selecting loss functions, with a focus on classification problems. We will demonstrate how certain properties of deep neural networks can simplify the optimization process, allowing the use of regularization techniques to maintain the network's predictions and features under various perturbations. This approach enables the construction of robust, regularization-based loss functions, and provides theoretical justification that networks trained with such loss functions generalize well. Experimental results will further illustrate the effectiveness of these proposed loss functions.

Describing the behavior of many-body systems is a complex task, with the term 'many-body correlations' serving as a comprehensive descriptor for their dynamics. To address this challenge, we focus on the parquet theory that seeks to describe these correlations efficiently. This approach reduces the complexity of their characterization to the most significant single particle correlations, namely the scattering matrices. Within the framework of the parquet theory, we can derive a set of integro-differential equations governing these scattering matrices. The term 'parquet theory' originates from the visual representation of the relationship between these matrices at different interaction levels, illustrating the connection between local and non-local aspects of the interactions. The non-local Kohn-Luttinger components of the scattering matrices can be expressed in terms of the local components through a set of simpler integro-differential equations.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been a subject of intense research for decades, and while examples of quantum Hall systems that demonstrate this phenomenon are well-documented (such as in GaAs and the Van der Waals material $NbSe_2$), we have recently discovered a distinct manifestation of exciton condensation in the quantum spin Hall system of $HgTe/Hg_{1-x}In_xTe$ heterostructures. Our findings reveal that the transition from semimetal to excitonic insulator is marked by the emergence of a temperature-dependent gap, which starts at the Dirac points of the electron and hole bands when an extremely low electron-hole carrier density ($n_{eh}=1.1\times10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$) exists. This dense density is 4 orders of magnitude higher than the critical exciton density ($n_{cr}=10^6$ cm$^{-2}$) found in $NbSe_2$.

To analyze the impact of an external magnetic field on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, we analyze magnetic susceptibility data using the Ginzburg-Landau theory, which allows for the calculation of critical temperature and field. This critical information then facilitates the determination of the superconducting gap structure, assuming a gapless d-wave model, within a momentum space approach that incorporates the Dirac points of the Fermi surface. By incorporating the effects of both Se and Fe layers, we analyze how these interface regions influence the superconducting gap, particularly at the surfaces, and investigate the resulting changes in magnetic susceptibility, surface and bulk contributions, and the surface band's influence in the absence of a magnetic field. Moreover, we also explore the impact of magnetic fields on both surface and bulk contributions and compare our findings to experimental observations of similar systems, including surface superconductivity, coexisting topological and superconducting properties, and topological surface states.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental results on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baseline models.

To study how music changes over time, an incremental approach is used to build up large music databases by layer by layer, and an analysis of the existing data is presented in this paper. The analysis focuses on ten characteristics of music and how they have changed from year to year. By taking a closer look at each feature, it's possible to understand their significance in the broader context of music theory and the music industry. The analysis includes looking at the data in the broader sense of two hundred years as well as the recent ten year period. The results of the analysis show interesting patterns in the data and provide an in-depth explanation of the findings.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves systems divided into numerous blocks or groups, where the likelihood that a new arrival will merge with an existing group is governed by a function dependent on the group's current size or 'wealth', rather than its historical development. This paper studies the long-term behavior of this model under the condition that the function is based solely on group size and utilizes tools and concepts from spectral analysis to demonstrate that, under specific circumstances, a significant proportion of the group's allocation will ultimately join one particular group, while others will undergo a different long-term evolution characterized by a power law distribution of group sizes, along with the associated fluctuation effects.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome, then utilizing these models to calculate TET, ATE, and the marginal treatment effect (MTE). While model-augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) and its variant, nAIPW, have been extensively utilized, they can still exhibit high bias and large variance. Differentiating themselves from existing methods, two new double machine learning (DML) estimators, extremely AIPW (eAIPW) and its variant, enAIPW, rely solely on four model-augmented IPR weights in their estimation process. Further analysis and simulations reveal both eAIPW and enAIPW have better large-sample and small-sample performance compared to existing methods. Additionally, both eAIPW and enAIPW have better performance than AIPW, nAIPW, TET, and MTE with simulations, achieving less bias and a smaller variance. The results also indicate enAIPW, with its combination of multiple model averaging, exhibits higher robustness.

Atmospheric circulation is simulated using a primitive equation model at a resolution of 96km with 30 vertical levels, focusing on understanding and improving a numerical framework for studying the formation and behavior of a single barotropic vortex on a beta-plane. The impact of various numerical schemes and horizontal viscosity adjustments is investigated, along with the model's response to atmospheric buoyancy and a terrain-following stretching scheme. By optimizing these factors, a generalized buoyancy-activation threshold and tuned numerical viscosity were found to yield a stable cyclogenesis and robust atmospheric connections with the ocean. This led to the emergence of a steady cyclogenesis frequency in experimental simulations. The resulting balance between forces was analyzed to explain the dynamic behavior of a barotropic vortex, and key physical processes were identified as vital to its maintenance, including a specific type of buoyancy gradient and the interaction with ocean currents. These elements were found to be essential in producing strong atmospheric and oceanic exchanges and a stable cyclogenesis frequency.

A typical approach to modelling extreme events involves considering a sequence of data and defining a threshold beyond which the excesses of this sequence are modelled using a classical exponential-type distribution, which is valid for sufficiently high threshold levels. However, finding the point above which the exponential-type distribution is valid can be challenging. It is often desirable to assume that certain model parameters are constant across various threshold levels. We will explore a different approach that uses a different distribution to model the "very large" values in a sequence, which has a more broad applicability than the traditional exponential-type distribution, while still maintaining the model parameter invariance across different threshold levels. This approach is particularly valuable when sample sizes are not sufficiently large for the traditional method to be effective. Furthermore, we will look at how this method can be adapted to time series data, taking into account possible serial correlation in the data.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in data-driven policy design. Our theoretical framework assumes a data matrix containing n tuples of (s, a, r, next_s) from the offline dataset, where s, a, r, next_s represent observations of the state, action, reward, and next state, respectively. Given δ as a confidence parameter, ε as a value function approximation error, and M as the value function mixer, our research establishes lower and upper bounds for adversarial robustness. We find that if the adversary modifies a fraction of the dataset, recovery is only possible up to a specific threshold of mistakes. Our research also explores the impact of data coverage and policy complexity on adversarial robustness.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

We're looking at artificial molecular motors that utilize electric currents to drive their operation. Although there's not much information on how they're actually used in practice, there's still questions surrounding their thermodynamic efficiency. To better understand this, we examine a specific type of molecular motor system, where we find that the presence or absence of electric currents leads to two unique pathways for achieving steady-state conditions. As a result, the rules for determining the direction and magnitude of currents that maximize operational performance vary depending on the current pathway. Furthermore, we found that the maximum power output of these systems is influenced by currents in a more complex way than previously thought.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional tables with entries drawn from a group $\Gamma$. Denoted as $\mathbb{F}_n$, the space of these tables is used to define the convolution of two functions through matrix multiplication across the table dimensions. Focusing on the problem of efficiently computing the convolution of two $k^m \times k^m$ tables with entries from a group of size $k$, where the parameter $m$ represents the problem dimension and $k$ represents the alphabet size. By analyzing a naive approach, we note its computational cost would be $((k^m)^2)$ operations in a total time complexity of $((k^m)^3))$. By introducing the parameter separation condition where $m$ is significantly larger than $k$, we explore alternative approaches. A key breakthrough involves a new formula for convolution that leverages the function $f_i(x)$ which maps each $n$-tuple to $\Gamma$, where $x$ is an $n$-tuple. This reformulation enables the convolution of $f_i(x)$ values with minimal operations, resulting in an improved time complexity of $((k^m)^3))$. However, this improvement is offset by a pre-processing step that takes $((k^m)^3))$ operations to compute the necessary values. This optimized approach is applied by estimating its effectiveness in solving the shortest path problem on a

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a more detailed analysis is required to understand its evolution within the solar neighborhood, which relies heavily on accurate modeling of its atmospheric conditions. Despite multiple spectroscopic studies, there remains significant disagreement regarding its model, especially when modern T-dwarf models are applied, resulting in discrepancies with earlier T-dwarf templates, especially in the 1-1.5 and 3.5-4 $\mu$m regions, where several key molecular bands are located. A newly developed radiative transfer code was used to create synthetic spectra and explore different atmospheric models through 36 different parameter combinations, revealing a unique and unambiguous best model, as well as a set of acceptable parameters that aligns with observational data within our understanding. Our analysis suggests a mass of approximately 26-133 $M_{Jup}$, a mass range consistent with previous studies. Our results indicate a surface temperature of 950-1100 K, significantly cooler than the 1100-1300 K surface temperature suggested by the 2011 study, as well as the 1200-1400 K model proposed in 2016, highlighting the need for further investigation into GJ 229B's atmospheric profile.

To search for the potential existence of a multiquark state, we employed the Gaussian Distributed Momentum Space (GDMS) model to analyze $\Lambda_b\rightarrow p K^-$ decays. The study was conducted for both $S$-wave and $L$-wave configurations. Given the current data constraints, we determined that any possible exotic state would have a mass under 2 GeV. However, we found that a dynamical decoupling of the $\Lambda_b\rightarrow p K^-$ decay from duality violations at low energies makes detecting an exotic state extremely challenging.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a particularly useful tool for detecting new physics. The primary obstacles in measuring these parameters are small branching fractions of the final-state particles and $\phi_{s}$'s small magnitude. The proposed $b\bar{b}$ factory, a high-energy collider with $b\bar{b}$ collision, is designed to eliminate these obstacles by accurately determining $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$. The proposed project discusses the feasibility of achieving this goal.

Airborne transmission of viruses like influenza, SARS, and COVID-19 can occur when contaminated aerosols are transported and inhaled, particularly within confined environments like rooms, buses, and subway cars where the airflow is influenced by temperature differences, air exchange, and fan placement. Our study develops a comprehensive model that incorporates building characteristics and airflow patterns to predict the force acting on particles as they move through the air. By combining this model with the Stokes force, which dictates particle movement, we can determine the locations and concentrations of particles within a given space. This theoretical framework is further applied to simulate the transport of virus-carrying aerosols in a defined room under four distinct air circulation scenarios: no convection, cold floor, warm floor, and general air circulation. These scenarios correspond to different thermal conditions and are compared, while also taking into account the release positions of particles and factors like deposition on surfaces, filtration, and the size and concentration of released virus-carrying particles. Our analysis identifies key variables that affect the average concentration of particles in the air, offering insights into the relative importance of airflow patterns for predicting and modeling airborne virus transmission, ultimately allowing us to estimate the basic reproduction number for specific situations.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay characteristics. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition from the $0_{1}^{+}$ state in $^{54}$Fe to various states in $^{54}$Mn, as well as $^{54}$Mn to the $0_{2}^{+}$ state in $^{54}$Fe. These experiments were carried out using the ISOLDE facility. Due to the involvement of odd-odd nuclei, calculating $\beta$-decay properties via shell-model computations requires incorporating both proton and neutron excitations. In this investigation, $\beta$-decay characteristics involving the $0_{1}^{+}$ and $0_{2}^{+}$ states in $^{54}$Fe were calculated using both the KB3G and O6M shell-model interactions. In terms of $\beta$-decay properties, calculations using the KB3G interaction are in better alignment with experimental results than those using the O6M interaction. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on previous research, which focused on the optimal execution of large multi-asset trade orders, by further investigating the application of double-sided auctions to request multiple quantities of assets. In this area, we demonstrate that the dual feasibility method can be adapted to handle multiple quantities, resulting in a modified algorithm. We test its performance using real data from the first tranche of a €1bn trade and observe that it outperforms single-sided auction strategies. Additionally, this work lays the foundation for future exploration of executing large multi-asset trade orders over shorter timeframes.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all phobic words of arbitrary character sets and numerous other specific patterns of interest.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges posed by high-dimensionality, complex modeling requirements, and the dynamics of implicit equations within a subspace. The least square method is commonly used to solve implicit equations, but its reliance on the L2-norm minimization leads to poor results in high-dimensionality. We introduce an alternative approach that incorporates the prior knowledge of the prior distribution and utilize the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence for estimating implicit equations. This methodology provides superior accuracy in learning implicit equations, particularly for solving the problems of Model Order Reduction and Computational Fluid Dynamics.

known as the opening repertory, holds significant influence on game outcomes.
Despite decades passing, new strategies continually emerge, and experienced players
adopt them to gain even a slight edge. Although human players possess collective
wisdom, their game approach becomes increasingly predictable towards the end of the
game phase. To tackle this, we introduce a network of chess opening strategies, where
nodes represent the game's initial phase and edges represent transitions between
successful games. By using algorithms from the small-world network theory, our
analysis reveals that this network shares common characteristics with other
complex systems. Additionally, the clusters formed allow us to identify popular
strategy combinations among top players. This data-rich framework not only offers
insights into optimal opening strategies but also provides a foundation for
practical applications, such as suggesting less explored but effective moves. Our
research also explores the evolution of chess strategy through statistical analysis,
highlighting the shift from purely human intelligence to intelligence augmented
by machine learning as strategies become more data-driven. Finally, the study of our
network will benefit computer science researchers, as it shares similarities with
other complex systems.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online access to three-dimensional (3D) models is crucial for
research and education in the 3D field and for promoting three-dimensional
technology adoption. Currently, retrieving 2D images through visual search is
common, but there's a lack of convenient methods for three-dimensional object
search in the 2D-3D bridge area. In this paper, a novel method based on hand
doodling in 2D for automatically acquiring 3D models in 2D hand-drawn search is
proposed. A VRLibrary called AirDoodle allows users to create sketches in 2D
while 3D objects move in 3D space. A neural network-based automatic 3D shape
reconstruction method called HandVNet is designed, which integrates hand-drawn
input with actual shape output using an encoder-decoder framework. A multi-level
hand-drawn feature extraction method using a hand-drawn map is introduced, which
utilizes a multi-scale hand-drawn feature extraction method. Additionally, the
method includes a guided 3D shape reconstruction method using a cycle-consistent
adversarial network. Experiments and evaluations of retrieval accuracy, ablation
tests, and comparisons with other methods have been conducted.

This report provides a detailed overview of the findings from KIC 8471454, an exoplanet with a highly eccentric orbit that receives the most extreme variations in solar energy. The investigation into this system began in 2013/2014, using multiple tools, including the Kepler, TESS, and ground-based telescopes. In addition to analyzing visible light, we also examined the radio spectrum. Our findings include the discovery of the exoplanet's orbit, which was initially thought to be different, as well as evidence of stellar flares and featureless radio emissions. Furthermore, analysis suggests the presence of two distinct active regions on the surface of the exoplanet.

We've analyzed the initial value problem for an ideal fluid sphere describing a star's collapse, focusing on how the equations of state and mass distribution affect the description of the fluid's behavior.
