This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions. The extensive dataset captures simultaneous hand, arm, torso, and foot movement from multiple angles to learn accurate zero-hand gesture prediction models. By creating simultaneous gestures across these body parts, the dataset aims to model the five fundamental body signals humans use to communicate. Employing an advanced gesture generation system, each gesture view in the dataset was carefully created to prevent motion interference and ensure natural expression. The dataset consists of simultaneous hand, arm, torso, leg, and foot movement captured from seven viewpoints using an advanced motion capture system. Utilizing the dataset allows research to advance through multigesture generation, modeling, and replication. The dataset can also be accessed to influence multigesture imitation, real-time generation, and body expression transfer tasks. The dataset represents simultaneous hand, arm, torso, leg, and foot movement across seven viewpoints.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, the transfer of neural models between languages can be labor-intensive and inefficient, requiring significant manual intervention. In response, we introduce a straightforward approach to transfer neural models without human input, leveraging the vast amount of parallel data available on the web. Our novel method, named SIAM, enables the simultaneous training of two neural models in multiple languages, effectively transferring knowledge from English to other languages. The results demonstrate that SIAM not only excels in transfer learning but also outperforms previous techniques in several tasks, including classification and named entity recognition, even with limited human annotations. Moreover, we explore the impact of SIAM on pre-trained models, noting a notable decrease in performance when combining SIAM with BERT. The source code for SIAM is publicly available on GitHub.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing video up-scaling techniques. BasicVSR leverages bidirectional attention modules to integrate the optical flow-guided feature alignment. We make two key contributions to this approach. First, we introduce a novel GPR module that propagates the feature alignment process to the second order grid, enhancing the alignment of video features across frames, and outperforming the prevailing optical flow-guided approach. Second, we develop a novel deformable alignment module that incorporates flow-guided and background-aligned deformable gradients, allowing the model to adaptively focus on background features and naturally align the current frame with the reference frame. Our model integrates the proposed GPR and FDBA modules with the existing bidirectional attention module to create the Enhanced VSR model. The new model is then used for self-supervised video up-scaling, achieving state-of-the-art performance and surpassing BasicVSR and other top video enhancement models with minimal or no motion compensation. Notably, the model only aligns the first frame for training, while the remaining frames are not aligned.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods that rely on task-related parameters,
it has been more challenging to reproduce in model-based approaches. We introduce
the first dependent vector-epsilon greedy policy for multi-task vectorized
reinforcement learning. By using a shared transition predictor, our dependent
gates utilize the parameters from its network to assign a prior probability to
each action space, thereby limiting the available actions. We designed and
validated a series of single- and multi-task benchmarks, illustrating the
positive impact of dependence on policy consistency and task performance, as
well as the occurrence of a early negative transfer. We also show the occurrence
of dependence through model-evaluation, a technique allowing for the comparison
of different shared predictors without the need for additional learning.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with the Markov chain approximation to evaluate the impact of energy scaling on the efficiency of the engines when subjected to temperature constraints. It was discovered under these conditions, the maximum efficiency was achieved when the protocol changed slowly over time but also within a specific time scale relative to the heat bath temperatures. Protocols maximizing efficiency were found to exhibit symmetry in the temperature differences they produced when the system reached a steady state. We have identified the conditions under which these protocols remain effective in the systems we studied and demonstrated the accuracy of our findings for a stochastic heat engine representing a particle moving in a viscous medium through a periodically changing landscape of energy barriers.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess the resilience of power infrastructure, the model evaluates the likelihood of power substations becoming disconnected, and reports the average duration of outages. By applying the model to a super-station, an example in Florida is presented, and the results are validated against historical data from Hurricane Ian.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. Can a next-generation collider, specifically a compact $e^+e^-$ accelerator with a 275 GeV center-of-mass energy, accurately verify the properties of the standard model's lightest neutral Higgs boson with sufficient precision? A detailed study of the optimal strategies for producing the desired signal at the collider in question, while minimizing background interference, has been conducted.

This research proposes an innovative approach called Pitch-Dependent Dilated Convolution Neural Networks for the task of monophonic audio autoencoding, enabling efficient low-loss audio generation over extended periods. We integrate pitch information from FM-Corner 2.0 into the network to enhance its capacity for accurate audio reconstruction. To handle long sequences, we employ a multi-rate architecture combining pitch and low-frequency branches with a high-resolution branch. Additionally, we evaluate various design choices for this model, including analysis of pitch representation and the impact of combining multiple convolutions. Our evaluation also involves state-of-the-art autoencoders such as PEA and PEA+, facilitating a comparison of their performance.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF) have become highly popular due to their effectiveness in managing large and growing amounts of data, but their performance can be hindered by the cold start and sparsity problems. The challenges of CF can be addressed through side information, a technique that combines CF with external data to enhance model accuracy. However, side information often fails to provide the necessary coverage, resulting in significant errors. To overcome this, a new method called Sparsely-Self-Normalizing Expanding Vector Machine (S-VEVM) has been developed. Relying on a single aspect ratio, S-VEVM defines a sparsity pattern for each user and item, effectively expanding the user item projection while accurately modeling user item aspects. The S-VEVM model can be trained using a logistic regression approach based on a Maximum Likelihood estimation that adjusts the aspect scores based on user interest and is supported by a Bayesian hyperparameter optimization method called Adaptive Sequential Sampling. The experiments, conducted on three public datasets, show that S-VEVM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in precision, recall and pinball loss metrics.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators is essential for advancing detection capabilities, and the star's outer atmosphere is accessible for spectral analysis. In this study, we employ synthetic observations of stellar prominences using the GARCON code, tailored for the James Webb Space Telescope and ground-based 8m class telescopes. The synthetic spectra incorporate observational realism, featuring the stellar spectrum, a realistic prominence structure from SDO/AIA observations, and physically accurate scattering processes. Our results show prominence scatterings with moderate amplitudes and broad line profiles, distinguishing them from atomic lines and noise patterns. These synthetic spectra are designed to replicate real observations and can be adapted for various star types and atmospheric conditions. By simulating a range of scenarios, we have successfully reproduced a observed cross-correlation function, and our analysis also reveals the potential for prominent features in mid-infrared wavelength range. These findings have implications for both Doppler detection and spectral feature interpretation in this range.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup causes the Majorana peak to broaden and shift to lower energies, ultimately disappearing as temperature drops, as indicated by research in [Phys. Rev. B 97, 115426 (2018)]. Conversely, non-Majorana peaks simply disappear with increasing temperature. Due to finite temperature effects causing the tunneling peak to intrinsically broaden, a high-resistance lead facilitates accurate identification of the peak's behavior at non-zero temperatures. We propose that a tunneling experiment utilizing leads with high resistance could serve as a more reliable means of verifying the presence of Majorana modes in hybrid superconductor-semiconductor nanowire setups.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes due to the lack of a unique solution. Our method leverages user feedback in the form of multiple reference images to provide a more accurate representation of the desired transformation. By combining multiple prior distributions into a single unified distribution, our approach prevents over-fitting and generalizes better than individual reference images on their own. Our framework employs a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) architecture to achieve these results. Our method's performance has been validated through experiments on various image editing benchmarks and is comparable to other state-of-the-art image editing techniques.

This technical report showcases the model that claimed second place in the CMKVG challenge, a large-scale competition focused on breaking down the complexities of understanding long videos. We developed a multi-task learning architecture that integrates text, image, and video information, with a particular emphasis on using text-guided aggregation and content-based text generation. The code for this model is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/hustved/CMKVG. Notably, our model achieved a score of 0.4267 in the final evaluation, surpassing the scores of 0.4101 and 0.4041 obtained during three separate rounds of testing.

This field research examines the dynamics of snow settling on the ground and its correlations with atmospheric turbulence features. The investigation into the vapor depositing on the surface and its connections to down-blowing atmospheric patterns has a long history. To examine this, the CONIFER array of weather stations was utilized to collect data on the ground and surrounding atmospheric turbulence over a period of 11 months. The data revealed that the concentration and dynamics of snow particles are heavily influenced by atmospheric vortex structures and their dimensions. Notably, these vortices tend to have smaller scales, around 20-60 meters, and during the winter seasons, the concentration of snow particles causes their density to drop by a factor of approximately 2.5. The theoretical framework suggests that this particular size of vortices creates a counter-productive effect, reducing the settling speed of snow particles by roughly 60%. The observed vortices in the CONIFER data range from 1-100 meters and their scales are consistent with those reported in previous research on snowy conditions. The findings are significant for the understanding of snow settling patterns and atmospheric turbulence on a local level.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool for creating simplified representations of the world, guiding the behavior of the user to effectively interact with their environment. This paper explores the potential of implementing the principles of active inference within the framework of cognitive architectures, focusing on its ability to represent and understand a dynamic environment, as well as the types of behavioral outcomes that ensure a person's survival and the types of perceptions they will continue to generate.

In experimental facilities with numerous sensors and vast amounts of data produced per second, real-time data acquisition is a significant challenge for high energy physics and cosmology researchers. To address this issue, new systems have been developed to analyze and utilize data immediately as it's being collected, often under significant computational pressure. Similarly, the field of streaming computing has emerged to handle massive data streams in real-time. This report compares the methodologies and tools available in both domains, including the Cisco NetFlow protocol, which serves as a unified data communication standard. It aims to illustrate the potential synergies between streaming computing and high energy physics/experimental cosmology applications, focusing on the integration of NetFlow as a data transport mechanism and exploring four specific data streaming use cases to demonstrate the feasibility of combining these technologies.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible, albeit hierarchically organized.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph is denoted as $(n,s,t)$, consisting of $n$ vertices and edges formed by subsets of $s$ vertices that contain $t$ vertices in their convex hull. Researchers have sought to determine the maximum number of these special edges within $(n,s,t)$ configurations. Previous work focused on specific cases where $t$ equals $2$ or $s$ is $4$, with this note addressing the remaining instance of $(n,4,2)$. The research finds a corresponding upper limit for this scenario, and as a result, establishes a broader exception-less bound applicable to all values of $s$ and $t$.

To obtain a precise description of light nuclear reaction cross sections, it is crucial to have an in-depth knowledge of the directly involved continuum states. Our study focuses on identifying the main contributions to the $\alpha$-particle production in the entrance channel of two significant nuclear reactions, $\pi^p e^+ \alpha$ and $\pi^{\alpha} e$, within the framework of the cluster model. By doing so, we can better understand and describe the structural characteristics of the $\alpha$-particle in this context. To achieve this, our approach involves employing a three-body variational method using the pseudo-spectroscopic cluster model. By analyzing our results, we can assess and refine our understanding of light nuclear reactions and the directly involved states. Our study reveals substantial differences in $\alpha$-particle structure between the two reactions and indicates varying structures within the same reaction. Moreover, these findings have significant implications for understanding how these nuclear reactions are influenced.

A previously published bio-inspired robot called the Lamprey-Robot (L-Robot) successfully mimicked the swimming movements of a living lamprey animal. After swimmng, the robot climbed into a dense forest. As it climbed a tree trunk using the same undulating motion as the living lamprey, the robot's in-water performance was compared to its actual performance. A simulated environment showed that both the robot and the animal could move forward at similar speeds in water and on trees. The L-Robot is now referred to as an amphibious robot.

A different type of viewing angle for another climbing robot was then presented. This robot used its flexible design to move between trees by dropping over edges, as opposed to climbing vertically. After climbing over a series of simulated obstacles, the climbing robot successfully navigated a real-world course.

Finally a new type of simulation was presented where an advanced agent used its brain, much like a human's, to control its body. This involved using its visual input to adjust its movements as needed. This method was shown to be successful in assisting a different type of robot with its brain to balance on top of trees by using its hand to interact with its environment.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation and influenced by Venusian stochastic forces. To account for measurements taken at discrete time intervals, a Fokker-Planck-Feynman framework is adopted, allowing the derivation of an information functional that evaluates the relationship between probabilistic models and empirical data. Ultimately, an optimal control problem based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence leads to a set of forward-backward stochastic differential equations, followed by the numerical implementation of the probabilistic model and the empirical data through the Monte Carlo method.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success in high-density environments with low device heights and short distances is challenging, particularly in mobile devices. Scheduling D2D communications effectively requires coordinating multiple simultaneous communications at D2D base stations to maximize overall throughputs and minimize end-to-end delay. However, due to individual D2D mobile devices having limited processing power and power supply, it is power-efficient for D2D communication management to be carried out by D2D base stations. A cross-layer, cognitive processing approach has been proposed to optimize D2D communication scheduling, incorporating packet aggregation and network coding at D2D base stations and scheduling in time and power at the radio interface, while also taking into account the impact of packetization delay and the power backoff time on end-to-end delay and total power consumption. Research has shown that finding the globally optimal solution is NP-hard and that an iterative algorithm, with two subproblems being jointly optimized via Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), achieves the greatest D2A throughput and end-to-end delay reduction. Finally, the proposed approach is experimentally validated in simulations, exhibiting superior performance over existing methods in terms of end-to-end delay, D2D throughput, and total power.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specific limit. They then adapted these findings to consider a slight modification in the potential and calculated the difference between the modified and original solutions, which led to a parameter-independent impedance formula.

Calculations of the impact of gravity on the dynamics and wave patterns of merging compact binary systems of non-spinning heavy bodies, with no smaller companions, are performed to the order of 3.5 post-Minkowskian and 3.555 post-Minkowskian interactions. This was accomplished by applying a洛朗 expansion to a previously computed scattering amplitude that includes interactions between bodies of various masses. The resulting wave patterns and their impacts on the systems' movements have been Compton-Wilson expanded to a specific order in the bodies' velocities, which matches the relevant post-Newtonian order for the desired precision. When these findings are applied to a particular case of interest, they are found to closely match the predictions based on the traditional method to the corresponding post-Newtonian order, demonstrating a high degree of agreement between the two approaches in predicting the effects of gravity on the systems' movements and the resulting wave patterns.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is achieved by utilizing an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The interaction between the LASE from the XFELO and the electron beam features two distinct interaction regions, or "humps," which allows for the simultaneous extraction of the benefits of XFELO seeding and undulator tapering. This results in the generation of extremely intense X-ray pulses, with an estimated output of ~10^19 W, a close match of 95% in frequency, and a sub-picosecond duration, made possible by the adaptable electron beam and the interaction of the LASE and electron beam.

Event identification is crucial for real-time monitoring of large, evolving networks. However, detecting events in dynamic graphs is a complex task, as these graphs not only experience the emergence and disappearance of nodes and connections, but their underlying data attributes also change over time. To address this challenge, we have developed a method that combines temporal subgraph extraction with supervised learning. By breaking down dynamic graphs into a series of sequential subgraphs, we enable the application of event detection using classification. To validate our approach, we created two novel datasets, the CSE3943 Log Analysis Dataset and the CSE4767 Network Traffic Dataset, based on real-world data. Following the extraction of these subgraphs, we utilized event detection algorithms, yielding significant success in classifying events with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.84 and an F1 score of 0.70.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps through histopathological analysis is a vital process for the development of diagnostic and predictive models that aid in the treatment of patients with colorectal cancer. In this study, a dataset consisting of 185 H&E-stained glass slides and 262 H&E-stained routine chromoendoscopy-guided biopsy clips was established. This dataset was divided into three categories: normal, serrated pathway-related, and malignant tissues. The normal category comprised 71 slides, while the serrated pathway-related category included 59 slides, and malignant tissue was represented by 55 datasets. The malignant category was further divided into adenocarcinoma (29 datasets) and benign non-serrated (26 datasets). A total of 65,222 pathologically annotated image patches and 1382 diagnostic reports were also prepared. The annotated patch data was utilized to train two models, ResNet50 and ResNet101, whereas the diagnostic reports were used to train a BERT language model. These three models demonstrated superior performance in characterizing and classifying colorectal polyps.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our analysis focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented as a source culling scheme consisting of two interconnected sources and a nulling encoder that selects output sequences from the primary source. This is complemented by a decoding encoder that maps sequences from the secondary source into the primary source's outcome space. This setup ensures that every primary source sequence has a matching sequence in the secondary source that decodes to it without error. However, this correspondence may also leak information to the adversary, whose ability to correctly guess the primary source sequence based on this leakage is measured. This leakage is quantified in terms of its maximum possible entropy. This study establishes a range of lower and upper bounds for this leakage in terms of the sizes of the sources. This will serve as a reference point for experimental evaluations of the actual amounts of leakage that occur in real-world scenarios.

Deep learning-based compressive sensing utilizes generative models trained on large datasets to predict comprehensive data from limited measurements. Two prominent approaches, which leverage a pre-trained model and perform additional optimization, were examined. A comparative analysis was performed using three different image types on two different CS problems. The results showed that the optimization-based method provides a noticeable improvement over the pre-trained model in generating detailed lung structures, while both approaches exhibit comparable performance in reconstructing cat images, and the optimization-based method yields slightly better results at a higher computational cost.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we apply a gradient-based method after each measurement.  The quantum circuit's unitary structure is adjusted using a series of carefully designed operations, which necessitate intermediate measurements and update the circuit accordingly.  The method uses a shared set of parameters for analogous gate groups.  The paper examines how these shared parameters influence the algorithm's performance.  The study is supported by experiments in both simulated and actual quantum environments.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, two pairs of intersection points are required, one pair for each ellipse. The distance between these points is calculated using the solution for system (2), utilizing co-rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$, especially when distinct intersection pairs are involved. The matrices in system (2) are quadratic, ensuring real solutions for their intersection points. The solution presents a comprehensive vector-based approach for calculating the overlap area of two arbitrary 2D ellipses.

In continuous-time reinforcement learning, the q-function has emerged as a crucial tool, yet existing results are often confined to the realm of Markov processes. This work extends the q-function and its associated instantaneous advantage function to a broader, non-Markov setting, resulting in new functions with distinct integral and differential equations. We also establish a connection between these functions and their discrete-time counterparts, revealing that the instantaneous advantage function is the continuous-time equivalent of state advantage. Furthermore, we interpret q-learning as a projection of this advantage function onto the space of instantaneous features. Finally, we adapt the TS-trust algorithm for continuous-time reinforcement learning, propose an elliptical variation, and offer convergence guarantees for the algorithm.

We examine magnetic excitations in the triangular lattice Hubbard model using a method that combines local and current operators, exploiting any resulting modeless states to infer the ground state's spin configuration. We apply this method to an equilateral triangle with a single hole, a basic framework for understanding doped, magnetic systems with lattice current. Our analysis employs a mean-field approach modified to eliminate these less significant state and a more precise numerical calculation. We also consider how a weak second hop and the Fermi surface, developed within this model, may influence these less significant states.

In this research, we address the difficulty of vertebra localization and identification in the context of advanced spinal disease or deformity. These conditions are often characterized by atypical structures or merged vertebrae, which hinder accurate radiological interpretation and make computer-assisted diagnosis a valuable tool. Our approach involves using region-specific feature representation and a new method to compare interbody spaces. This technique, which leverages coarse-to-fine, difference-of-convex optimization, is designed to be robust and adaptable to varying image sizes. Additionally, we introduce a novel method for identifying adjacent vertebrae based on their topological relationships. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the V4S challenge dataset and is versatile enough to be applied to similar anatomical localization tasks. For demonstration purposes, we outline a end-to-end pipeline for automated vertebral labeling.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are computed as multi-time correlation functions of the underlying process. The cumulant-generating functions used in this context are derived from generating functions but suffer from a lack of gauge invariance. The work presented here proposes an alternative approach, redefining the cumulant-generating functions in terms of gauge-invariant objects, thereby facilitating further analysis. The benefits of this reformulation are utilized in examples, including showing how higher-order correlation functions can be expressed as sums of lower-order correlation functions.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through the topological transformation of one I-function to another. Furthermore, it explores and verifies the properties of this relative I-function relationship through specific examples.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy through an interaction known as coupled elastic oscillation. Our study investigates the transfer of energy between the materials at its resonant frequency and the concurrent transmission of photons and phonons. We utilize piezoelectric crystals as the two interacting solids and an external laser to induce mechanical oscillations in one of the crystals. When the crystals' internal phonon populations are in phase with the laser's population of photons, the system exhibits the principles of quantum electrodynamics. We explore how this principle can be applied to develop stable sources of entangled photon-phonon pairs and quantum acoustic devices.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on modern micro-LED technology to overcome size limitations inherent in conventional laser-based approaches. The proposed technique involves the use of a single, off-center excitation beam that gives rise to a standing wave pattern, the sides of which induce spatial variations in excitonic reservoir concentrations. The resulting density gradients drive polaritons and their corresponding reservoirs into coherent spatial patterns through diffusive motion. The observed reservoir patterns persist for hundreds of nanoseconds, well beyond typical light exposure times. The reservoir concentrations significantly influence polariton bundle particle distributions, thereby offering a dynamic and adjustable platform for shaping polariton spatial arrangements. The presented micro-LED-based method opens the door to creating complex patterns of polariton condensates and could be adapted for broader applications in spin-orbit physics, quantum optics, and related fields.

The disintegrating planet K2-22b, with a tiny dust tail, has unique characteristics. Although proposed explanations for its disintegration include thermal pressure from the hot planet and tidal forces due to its short orbital period, a detailed study of dust dynamics requires more information about these factors. Data from spectroscopy, orbital calculations, and physical properties of disintegrating stars and asteroids suggest that a dust disk model can be used to analyze disintegrating planets. This study found that a disk with sharp edges and an uneven surface brightness distribution can fit transmission and transmission-transmission spectroscopy data of disintegrating planets. Further investigation using this disk model to analyze disintegrating planet data, along with considerations of radiation pressure and tidal forces, revealed that wide disks with extended edges can reproduce transmission and transmission-transmission spectroscopy data of disintegrating planet with a fit. This finding suggests that tidal forces and radiation pressure can balance each other in this disintegrating planet. This study also discovered that transmission data can be used to analyze disintegrating planets and detect differences in dust grain properties based on transmission and transmission-transmission spectroscopy data of disintegrating planet. This finding suggests that disintegrating planet K2-22b may be undergoing a significant disintegration process and could potentially evolve into a black hole.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple specialized components, each containing essential data manipulation tools. As a versatile solution, Daany can be integrated into application development projects, extension creation (including Visual Studio plugins), or used independently for data processing tasks.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that his actual contribution was more complex. It is true that he had an exceptional command of mathematics, but this did not initially lead him to believe that nature could be understood through mathematical equations. Instead, he used mathematics primarily as a practical tool in his experiments. Over time, however, as he applied mathematical reasoning to physics, he began to develop the idea that the principles of nature are inherently mathematical in nature. This shift in perspective allowed him to discover that the properties of moving objects could be described using geometric concepts, such as triangles, which he believed were found in nature. This change in perspective had a profound impact on science, experiment, and education, influencing how we understand the relationship between mathematics and the natural world.

The increasing use of non-equilibrium methods in studying ionization in cosmological shocks and astrophysical contexts is largely driven by their computational efficiency and physical clarity.  A recent study by Bolton et al.  (2021) introduced a groundbreaking approach to determining hydrogen ionization fractions through an energy-based balance equation.  They built upon this method to develop generalized thermodynamic properties that offer a deeper understanding of ionization, shock behavior, and phase separation.  In this note, we provide a thorough derivation of these generalized thermodynamic properties, offering new insights into their biological and physical applications.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adapted Embedded Resolving patches for Kinetics (MACK) approach to bridge the disparity between fluid and kinetic representations. We implement this approach in the Open-source Code with Coherent capabilities, leading to a method that allows the use of kinetic solvers within a magnetohydrodynamic domain. We have developed and tested an adapted version of the Hybrid code (Hybrid-NB), featuring embedded kinetic ions in a magnetohydrodynamic electron domain. These modified simulations demonstrate a significant reduction in computational costs, achieving a 40% speedup over its original counterpart. Our research into the exact mass threshold in collisionless magnetic reconnection, a critical aspect of these kinetic models, yields intriguing findings. We have identified a mass ratio below which the electron magnetic ridge is unable to maintain magnetohydrodynamics, leading to magnetic reconnection that mimics pure fluid behavior.

This document explores digital assistants as learning tools, with implications for distributed cognition and user skill development. In professionally demanding fields, units work in line with strict protocols and learn from their errors, leading to shared knowledge that can be accessed through remembrance or documentation. We envision a digital assistant system analogous to experienced peers who, like a second brain, contribute to task execution while also facilitating user learning through discussion and error analysis. This document outlines a framework for designing such assistants and explores three digital contexts for error-based learning experiences, along with research questions and further research directions in digital assistants and expertise.
